from: Which aircraft has priority over the others in converging situations?
to: In converging situations, which statement about right of way is correct?
reason: The keyed answer (a towing aircraft has priority over the others) and its explanation ('all aircraft give way to those towing') are wrong under SERA.3210(c)(2)(iv): only power-driven aircraft must give way to an aircraft seen towing. A tug is itself power-driven and gives way to balloons, gliders and airships, which made the source option C ('a balloon over everything') at least as defensible as the key. Reworded so exactly one statement is true; same concept, same key (B).

from: A glider over a balloon
to: A glider has priority over a converging balloon
reason: See the question correction for id 6.

from: An aeroplane towing another aircraft or object
to: A power-driven aircraft gives way to an aircraft that is towing
reason: See the question correction for id 6.

from: A balloon over everything
to: A balloon gives way to a glider converging with it
reason: See the question correction for id 6.

from: A helicopter
to: A helicopter has priority over a converging aeroplane
reason: See the question correction for id 6.

from: all aircraft give way to those towing. (Balloons have priority over gliders, not "everything".)
to: SERA.3210: power-driven aircraft give way to aircraft seen to be towing other aircraft or objects. Otherwise, power-driven heavier-than-air aircraft give way to airships, gliders and balloons; airships give way to gliders and balloons; gliders give way to balloons.
reason: See the question correction for id 6.

from: Flashing white on the ground = return to the starting point on the aerodrome. It is the only white signal in the gun code.
to: Flashing white on the ground = return to the starting point on the aerodrome. It is not the only white signal: in flight, flashing white means land at this aerodrome and proceed to the apron.
reason: False claim. SERA Appendix 1 also gives a series of white flashes to an aircraft in flight: land at this aerodrome and proceed to the apron.
The 3-year validity of instructor certificates is FCL.940 (validity of instructor certificates); FCL.940.FI covers FI revalidation and renewal.

from: (a) 50 h instruction incl. 15 h in last 12 months; (b) instructor refresher seminar; (c) assessment of competence.
to: (a) 50 h of flight instruction during the validity period; (b) instructor refresher training (formerly a seminar); (c) an assessment of competence in the 12 months before expiry (FCL.940.FI).
reason: FCL.940.FI(a) has no '15 h in the last 12 months' condition for an FI(A). The only recency split is that 10 of the 50 h must be IR/BIR instruction in the last 12 months when IR/BIR instruction privileges are revalidated. The regulation now calls (b) refresher training.

from: 50 h instruction, of which 15 h in the 12 months before expiry
to: 50 h instruction during the validity period of the certificate
reason: The keyed option stated a requirement that is not in FCL.940.FI(a)(1)(i). Same key (B), corrected content.

from: Revalidation option (a): 50 h of instruction in the validity period, of which 15 h in the last 12 months. The 15 h recency prevents a 'front-loaded' claim.
to: Revalidation option (a): at least 50 h of flight instruction as FI, TRI, CRI, IRI, MI or examiner during the validity period (FCL.940.FI). Only if IR or BIR instruction privileges are being revalidated must 10 of those 50 h be IR/BIR instruction within the 12 months before expiry.
reason: See the option correction for id 73.

from: Minimum total flight time to start an FI(A) course (CPL holder):
to: Minimum total flight time to start an FI(A) course as a PPL(A) holder (no CPL):
reason: FCL.915.FI(b): the 200 h / 150 h PIC requirement is the PPL(A) route. A CPL(A) holder meets the prerequisite simply by holding the CPL, so the question as written had the routes the wrong way round. Same key (C).

from: FI(A) entry: 200 h total incl. 150 h PIC (CPL route). This is why the check-ride/pre-entry test matters.
to: FI(A) entry via a PPL(A): 200 h on aeroplanes or TMGs, including 150 h as PIC, plus a pass in the CPL theoretical knowledge examinations (FCL.915.FI(b)(2)). A CPL(A) holder meets this prerequisite by holding the CPL.
reason: See the question correction for id 76.

from: Class 1 medical validity for a pilot under 40 (commercial single-pilot, no passengers-over-60 restriction):
to: Class 1 medical validity for a pilot under 40, including single-pilot commercial operations with passengers:
reason: The age-60 limit in MED.A.045 is the pilot's age, not the passengers'. Reworded so the question does not suggest otherwise. Same key (B).

from: 6 months if 40+ (and for single-pilot CAT with passengers over 60).
to: 12 months (MED.A.045). It drops to 6 months for a pilot aged 40 or over in single-pilot commercial air transport carrying passengers, and for any pilot aged 60 or over.
reason: The source said 6 months applies to every pilot aged 40+ and to 'passengers over 60'. MED.A.045: 6 months only for a pilot aged 40+ in single-pilot CAT with passengers, or any pilot aged 60+.

from: full deflection below Va can't exceed load limits.
to: at or below Va a single full deflection of one control should not exceed the limit load — but repeated, alternating or combined full deflections still can.
reason: Overstated. Va protects only against a single full deflection of one control; alternating or combined inputs can still overstress the structure (the reason the FAA revised the Va guidance after AA587).

from: magnetos still fire; flaps are manual on most C152 (confirm).
to: magnetos still fire; the C152's flaps are electric and run on the battery once the alternator fails (confirm in your POH).
reason: C152 flaps are electric (flap switch lever, 15 A FLAP circuit breaker — 1978 POH Section 7, and this repository's own POH-sourced C152 bank).

from: Yaw (adverse)
to: Yaw
reason: The further effect of aileron is yaw toward the lower wing (sideslip plus weathercocking), not adverse aileron yaw, which is a separate effect in the opposite direction. Same key (B).

from: Further effect of aileron: yaw (adverse yaw), because the down-going aileron creates more drag; use rudder to balance.
to: Further effect of aileron: yaw toward the lower wing — the bank causes a sideslip and the fin and fuselage yaw the nose into it. Adverse aileron yaw (extra drag from the down-going aileron) is a separate effect, balanced with rudder.
reason: See the option correction for id 207.

to: B
reason: Wrong key. C152 flaps are electric, not manual: the flap switch lever on the instrument panel drives an electric motor, protected by a 15 A FLAP circuit breaker (1978 POH Section 7, and this repository's own POH-sourced C152 bank).
